card: Paper card. Question: Whether it is necessary to use all five elements (Hf, Nb, Ta, Ti, Zr) to achieve a random solid solution and good mechanical properties, or if reducing the system to 3 or 4 elements yields similar results.. System: HfNbTaTiZr system; specific alloys: HfNbTaTiZr (5-element), NbTaTiZr, NbTaTi, NbTiZr, TaTiZr, Nb0.5TaTiZr1.5, Nb1.5TaTiZr0.5 (3 and 4-element MEAs).. Processing: Vacuum arc melting in a water-cooled copper crucible; elements with 99.9% purity; ingots cast 8 times and flipped for mixing; no Hot Isostatic Pressing (HIP) or heat treatment applied to cast material.. Test conditions: Room temperature tensile testing with a strain rate of 2 × 10−4 s−1; Vickers hardness HV30 measurements; microstructure and phase analysis via SEM, WDS, and XRD.. Findings: The 5-element HfNbTaTiZr alloy exhibits the best combination of strength and elongation among all studied alloys.; The 4-element NbTaTiZr alloy has similar strength to the 5-element alloy but reduced elongation to 6.4%.; The TaTiZr alloy exhibited brittle behavior, breaking before reaching the yield point.; The NbTaTi alloy showed the highest elongation and the lowest hardness of 246 HV.; Simultaneous presence of Ta and Zr resulted in a significant reduction of ductility due to a reduction in BCC1 phase content.; Precipitation of Ta-rich particles on grain boundaries reduced maximum elongation to failure to zero values in brittle alloys.; A clear linear relationship exists between total elongation and the BCC1 phase content.; Grain size was estimated around 0.5 mm for all alloys except NbTiZr, which showed no dendritic segregation.. Mechanism: The simultaneous presence of Ta and Zr causes segregation during solidification due to a miscibility gap in the Ta-Zr binary phase diagram, leading to the formation of two BCC phases (BCC1 and BCC2) and intergranular Ta-rich precipitates. The reduction in the BCC1 phase content and the presence of these precipitates on grain boundaries are responsible for the significant reduction in ductility and the transition to brittle fracture.. Limitations: The study did not investigate the BCC2 and BCC3 phases or intergranular precipitates in detail. The relation between hardness and the misfit parameter δ is complicated because not all alloys are single-phase. The role of rapid cooling versus chemical composition in phase stability requires further verification.. Future work: Further research shall focus on detailed investigations of the BCC2 and BCC3 phases and intergranular precipitates. The destabilizing effect of Ta + Zr on BCC phase stability during manufacturing and aging shall be verified. The stabilizing effect of Hf on HCP phase formation during mid-temperature aging and the influence of cooling rate on phase composition shall be investigated.. Quote: "Simultaneous presence of Ta and Zr in the alloy resulted in a significant reduction of ductility caused by reduction of the BCC phase content."

W2889826453.title: Spark plasma sintering of gas atomized high-entropy alloy HfNbTaTiZr

card: Paper card. Question: Can high-entropy effects be utilized to induce a significant glass-to-glass transition in metallic glasses, and what are the structural and thermodynamic mechanisms behind this phenomenon?. System: Equiatomic NbNiZrTiCo high-entropy metallic glass (HEMG), with comparative systems NbNiZrTiCu and NbNiZrTiCoCu. Processing: Arc melting of pure elements (Nb, Ni, Zr, Ti, Co, Cu; purity ≥ 99.9 wt.%) under high-purity argon, followed by remelting five times; ribbon production via melt-spinning at a wheel surface velocity of 32 m s−1; heat treatment by heating to 855 K (TA) at 20 K min−1 and cooling at 20 K min−1. Test conditions: Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) at heating rates of 10–50 K min−1 and Flash DSC at >1000 K s−1; in-situ synchrotron X-ray diffraction from 305 K to 803 K at 30 K min−1; nanoindentation; dynamic mechanical analysis (DMA); atom probe tomography (APT) at 65 K; high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) at 200 kV. Findings: The as-prepared NbNiZrTiCo HEMG exhibits an enormous exothermic peak at 781 K with a heat release of 1.65 kJ mol−1, which is approximately 130% of the subsequent crystallization exotherm (1.27 kJ mol−1).; The glass-to-glass transition is irreversible; the heat-treated sample shows a distinct glass transition temperature (Tg) at ~764 K and lacks the first exothermic peak observed in the as-prepared state.; Nanoindentation measurements reveal a drastic increase in hardness from 6.78 GPa to 9.46 GPa (approximately 40% increase) after the transition.; In-situ synchrotron X-ray diffraction shows a significant non-linear shift of the first peak in the total structure function S(Q) and a narrowing of the full width at half maximum (FWHM) during the transition.; Pair-distribution function (G(r)) analysis indicates a contraction of short-range atomic distances (r11 and r12 shift to low-r) and prominent splitting of the second peak, signifying enhanced short- and medium-range ordering.; Atom probe tomography confirms a uniform element distribution at the sub-nanometer scale in both as-prepared and heat-treated samples, excluding spinodal decomposition.; The calculated lower limit of entropy change (ΔSH−L) for the transition is −1.96 J mol−1 K−1, with a corresponding enthalpy change (ΔHH−L) of −1.65 kJ mol−1.; Substituting Co with Cu to form NbNiZrTiCu (maintaining high excess configurational entropy) and adding Cu to form NbNiZrTiCoCu both result in similar glass-to-glass transitions.. Mechanism: The authors propose that the high configurational entropy (SC) and high excess configurational entropy (SE) dynamically stabilize a high-energy glass state during rapid vitrification by hindering atomic reconstruction and slowing diffusion. Upon heating, this high-energy state undergoes a thermodynamically driven transition to a low-energy, more ordered glass state, releasing a large amount of heat. The transition is driven by the specific combination of high SC and high SE (related to atomic size misfit), which enables the formation of a high-energy glass that is distinct from conventional metallic glasses.. Limitations: The text notes that the observed phase transition is an irreversible process, meaning the calculated entropy change represents a lower limit. Additionally, the detailed structural changes cannot be fully resolved by atom probe tomography due to its limited spatial resolution, and some weak diffraction peaks in crystallized samples could not be identified.. Future work: The authors suggest that the HEMGs may serve as model materials for exploring glass-to-glass transitions and the fundamental nature of glasses in materials science and condensed-matter physics. They also propose potential applications as energetic materials due to the large anomalous exotherm, which could contribute to combustion heats and lower ignition temperatures.. Quote: "An unusual glass-to-glass phase transition is discovered during heating with an enormous heat release even larger than that of the following crystallization at higher temperatures."

card: Paper card. Question: What is the role of vibrational contributions in the thermodynamic stability of high-entropy carbides, and under what conditions should they be included in stability predictions?. System: (HfNbTaTiV)C, (HfNbTaTiW)C, and (HfNbTaTiZr)C (referred to as HEC-V, HEC-W, and HEC-Zr). Processing: Computational integration of the Partial Occupation (POCC) algorithm with the AFLOW Automatic Phonon Library (APL); structures relaxed until forces were below 10−3 eV/ℓ; phonon calculations used a displacement magnitude of 0.015 ℓ in supercells with at least 180 atoms; TPOCC set to 2473 K.. Test conditions: Harmonic approximation at temperatures ranging from 0 K to synthesis temperatures; comparison against binary carbide precursors (rock-salt phases) and decomposition products; Debye-Grüneisen model (AGL) used for comparison.. Findings: Vibrational contributions shift the transition temperature for HEC-W by approximately 150 K, whereas they have only a small effect on HEC-V and HEC-Zr.; Mass disorder on the cation sublattice destabilizes the high-entropy carbides (increases vibrational free energy), while force constant disorder has a stabilizing effect.; The vibrational entropy change (ΔSvib) for HEC-W is 0.22 kB/atom, which is an order of magnitude larger than the 0.04 kB/atom observed for HEC-V and HEC-Zr.; The Debye-Grüneisen model (AGL) incorrectly predicts HEC-V to be more strongly stabilized by vibrations than HEC-W, failing to capture phonon anomalies present in VC.; Vibrational contributions shift the decomposition phase transition temperatures for HEC-V and HEC-W to lower temperatures by 80 K and 160 K, respectively.; The carbide sublattice distorts to accommodate different metal cations, resulting in nearest-neighbor metal-carbon distances that are closer to the average of binary carbides to maximize configurational entropy.; Vibrations alone are insufficient to stabilize HEC-V against decomposition at 2000 K, as the vibrational free energy change is smaller than the distance to the convex hull.. Mechanism: The authors argue that vibrational contributions are significant when precursors or decomposition products have different nearest-neighbor environments or symmetries compared to the high-entropy carbide. Specifically, the lower symmetry of hexagonal WC compared to the rock-salt HEC-W leads to depressed vibrational entropy in the precursor, creating a large stabilization gain upon forming the disordered phase. Conversely, when precursors and the HEC share similar atomic environments (as in HEC-V and HEC-Zr), the vibrational entropy changes are minimal.. Limitations: The study relies on the harmonic approximation, ignoring anharmonic effects which become significant at high temperatures and could stabilize structures with imaginary frequencies; the calculations use the PBE functional which may affect phonon frequencies; the ideal high-temperature configurational entropy is used, which overestimates entropic contributions at lower temperatures; and the study is limited to stoichiometric samples without accounting for vacancies or interstitial carbon.. Future work: The authors suggest that anharmonic contributions should be included to improve accuracy, that the effect of the exchange-correlation functional (e.g., SCAN vs. PBE) on transition temperatures needs investigation, and that defects such as vacancies and interstitial carbon atoms should be explored in future research on high-entropy ceramics.. Quote: "The contribution of vibrations to the stability of high-entropy ceramics is still controversial."

Paper card. Question: How to generate and validate derivative structures for (HfNbTaTi)RC high-entropy carbides to ensure converged vibrational free energy calculations.. System: (HfNbTaTi)RC where R = V, W, Zr. Processing: Created 49 ordered representative structures using the AFLOW-POCC algorithm from a rock-salt parent structure (space group: Fm-3m, #225); KPPRA value increased until vibrational free energy at 300 K converged within 1 meV/atom; APL supercells generated using standard conventional representations; relaxation and static calculations performed with exact same k-point densities.. Test conditions: Vibrational free energy convergence target of 1 meV/atom at 300 K; k-point densities required to be identical for relaxation and static calculations to avoid residual force increases.. Findings: 49 ordered representative structures were created for the (HfNbTaTi)RC system.; KPPRA values were increased until vibrational free energy at 300 K was converged within 1 meV/atom.; Using different k-point densities for relaxation and static calculations leads to an increase in residual forces by up to two orders of magnitude.; This residual force increase was observed even at KPPRA values above 20,000.; Standard conventional representations were used to generate APL supercells to achieve a more spherical shape.. Mechanism: The authors argue that maintaining exact same k-point densities for relaxation and static calculations is critical to prevent large residual forces, which can occur even at high KPPRA values if densities differ.. card: Paper card. Question: How does the addition of Germanium (Ge), in synergy with Ti, Cr, Al, and Hf, affect the oxidation resistance, pest oxidation susceptibility, and scale formation of Nb-silicide based alloys at 800 °C and 1200 °C compared to alloys without Ge?. System: Nb-18Si-5Ge (ZF1), Nb-18Si-10Ge (ZF2), Nb-24Ti-18Si-5Ge (ZF3), Nb-24Ti-18Si-5Cr-5Ge (ZF4), Nb-24Ti-18Si-5Al-5Ge (ZF5), Nb-24Ti-18Si-5Al-5Cr-5Ge (ZF6), and Nb-24Ti-18Si-5Al-5Cr-5Ge-5Hf (ZF9). Processing: Arc melting high purity elements in a copper water-cooled crucible under high purity argon atmosphere; each alloy turned over five times; samples cut to 3 × 3 × 3 mm3 and ground to 1200 grit. Test conditions: Isothermal oxidation in air at 800 °C and 1200 °C for 100 h; heating and cooling rates of 3 degrees per min. Findings: Alloys ZF1, ZF2, and ZF3 suffered from catastrophic pest oxidation at 800 °C, disintegrating into powder after 1 h (ZF1, ZF2) and 10 h (ZF3).; The addition of Ge substantially improved oxidation resistance, reducing the oxidation rate constant of ZF3 from 5.6 × 10−6 g·cm−2·s−1 (without Ge) to 2.7 × 10−7 g·cm−2·s−1.; At 800 °C, alloys ZF4, ZF5, ZF6, and ZF9 followed parabolic kinetics with total mass changes of 1.8, 3.1, 0.9, and 0.6 mg·cm−2 respectively after 100 h.; At 1200 °C, all tested alloys (ZF4-ZF9) exhibited two-stage kinetics: parabolic for the first 20-35 h followed by linear kinetics due to scale spallation.; The scale on alloy ZF9 at 800 °C was approximately 1 μm thick, which is 1/50, 1/13, and 1/8 of the thickness of scales formed on ZF4, ZF5, and ZF6 respectively.; Diffusion zones contaminated by oxygen (Nbss ~21.6-32 at.% O, Nb5Si3 ~2.4-2.6 at.% O) formed below the scale in ZF4 and ZF5, but no diffusion zone formed in ZF6 and ZF9.; Alloy ZF9 exhibited the best oxidation behavior at 800 °C with the lowest mass change (0.6 mg·cm−2), while ZF6 showed the best behavior at 1200 °C with the lowest metal recession rate (3.95 µm h−1).; The addition of Ge reduced the volume percentage of the Nbss phase in the ZF series alloys compared to similar alloys without Ge.. Mechanism: The suppression of pest oxidation and improved oxidation resistance are attributed to the synergy of Ge with Ti, Cr, and Al, which reduces the volume fraction of the Nbss phase and alters the oxide scale composition to include protective niobates (CrNbO4, AlNbO4) and GeO2. The formation of GeO2 in SiO2 creates a glass with high fluidity that can heal cracks. Scale spallation at 1200 °C is caused by stress accumulation due to the high Pilling Bedworth Ratio (2.68) of Nb2O5. The superior performance of ZF9 at 800 °C is linked to the synergy of Hf and Ge further reducing the Nbss volume fraction and optimizing the parameters δ and VEC.. Limitations: The study notes that Ge in synergy with Al, Cr, and Hf cannot eliminate scale spallation at 1200 °C. Additionally, the direct comparison with Refractory Metal High Entropy Alloys is limited by differences in temperature, atmosphere, duration, and microstructure.. Future work: The authors suggest further investigation into the synergy of specific alloying additions to control the volume fraction of solid solution and stabilize specific phases to eliminate pest oxidation and scale spallation.. Quote: "Only the alloys ZF1, ZF2, and ZF3 suffered from pest oxidation at 800 °C."

Paper card. Question: How does the addition of Germanium (Ge) and other alloying elements affect the oxidation resistance and microstructure of Nb-silicide based alloys compared to similar alloys without Ge and to Refractory Multi-Component High Entropy Alloys (RM HEAs)?. System: Nb-18Si-5Ge (ZF1), Nb-18Si-10Ge (ZF2), Nb-24Ti-18Si-5Ge (ZF3), Nb-24Ti-18Si-5Cr (ZF4), Nb-24Ti-18Si-5Al (ZF5), Nb-24Ti-18Si-5Al-5Cr-5Ge (ZF6), Nb-24Ti-18Si-5Al-5Cr-5Ge-5Hf (ZF9), and RM HEAs such as NbCrMo0.5Ta0.5TiZr and NbCrMoTiAl0.5. Processing: As-cast alloys; Isothermal oxidation in air at 800 °C and 1200 °C for 100 h; Cyclic oxidation in air at 1100 °C for about 500 h. Test conditions: Isothermal oxidation in air at 800 °C and 1200 °C for 100 h; Cyclic oxidation in air at 1100 °C for a total time of about 500 h. Findings: Only alloys ZF1, ZF2, and ZF3 suffered from catastrophic pest oxidation at 800 °C.; Ge addition substantially improved the oxidation resistance of the other alloys both at 800 °C and 1200 °C.; The mass change of the RM HEA NbCrMo0.5Ta0.5TiZr at 1000 °C was 120 mg·cm−2, compared with 0.55 and 41 mg·cm−2 of ZF9 at 800 and 1200 °C respectively.; The thickness of the scale on NbCrMo0.5Ta0.5TiZr was 1750 μm, about four times that of ZF9.; The oxidation of alloys ZF4, ZF5, ZF6, and ZF9 followed parabolic kinetics at 800 °C.; At 1200 °C, the oxidation of ZF4, ZF5, ZF6, and ZF9 followed parabolic kinetics in the early stages and linear kinetics at longer times.; Diffusion zones were formed below the scale/substrate interface only in alloys ZF4 and ZF5.; The addition of Ge reduced the vol % of the Nbss compared to Nb-silicide based alloys without Ge.. Mechanism: The superior oxidation behaviour of alloy ZF9 compared to RM HEAs was attributed to its higher and lower values respectively of the parameters δ and VEC. The addition of Ge reduced the volume percentage of the Nbss phase. The oxidation resistance of RM HEAs and Nb-silicide based alloys improves with increasing δ and decreasing VEC.. Limitations: At 1200 °C there was spallation of their scales. Cracks parallel to the scale/substrate interface were observed in the Nb5Si3 in alloys ZF4 and ZF5. The Nbss and Nb5Si3 in the diffusion zones were contaminated by oxygen. The Cr addition had an adverse effect on the mechanical behaviour of the scales.. Quote: "The Ge addition substantially improved the oxidation resistance of the other alloys both at 800 °C and 1200 °C."

W2969378216.title: On The Microstructures and Hardness of The Nb-24Ti-18Si-5Al-5Cr-5Ge and Nb-24Ti-18Si-5Al-5Cr-5Ge-5Hf (at.%) Silicide Based Alloys

card: Paper card. Question: Which powder metallurgy processing route (CIP+sintering, HIP, swaging, or SPS) combined with subsequent deformation (HPT) yields a fully dense, single-phase HfNbTaTiZr high entropy alloy with refined microstructure and acceptable mechanical properties?. System: HfNbTaTiZr equiatomic high entropy alloy. Processing: Three initial powder types were used: (1) Elemental powders mixed for 10 h at 45 rpm, cold isostatically pressed (CIP) at 400 MPa, then sintered at 1400 °C for 16 h; (2) Mechanically alloyed (MA) powders milled for 42 h; (3) Gas atomized (AT) powders. Sintering was performed at 1400 °C for 16 h in vacuum. Hot Isostatic Pressing (HIP) was at 1400 °C for 2 h under 190 MPa. Swaging was at 950 °C with an envelope of beta-titanium alloy. Spark Plasma Sintering (SPS) was at 1300 °C for 2 min under 80 MPa. High Pressure Torsion (HPT) was at room temperature with 2.5 GPa pressure and 15 revolutions.. Test conditions: Vickers hardness measured with 98.1 N load (ISO 6507); microstructure analyzed via LM, SEM (BSE mode), and XRD (Cu Kα); oxygen content measured by gas fusion; porosity determined by image analysis; positron lifetime spectroscopy used for defect characterization.. Findings: Swaging of sintered specimens resulted in cracking and failure, preventing full densification.; SPS of mechanically alloyed (MA) powders produced a fully dense but brittle specimen with high oxygen content (~1.07 wt %).; SPS of gas atomized (AT) powder with low oxygen content (~0.12 wt %) resulted in a fully dense, single-phase bcc specimen.; High pressure torsion (HPT) of the AT-SPS specimen refined the grain size from ~50 μm to below 500 nm (0.5 μm).; The AT-SPS-HPT specimen achieved a hardness of 410 HV10 (Abstract) and 584 HV10 (Section 4.3), attributed to grain refinement and dislocation density exceeding 5 × 10^14 m^-2.; Samples processed via CIP followed by HIP exhibited significantly lower hardness (~150 HV10) due to incomplete dissolution of elements and lack of a single-phase random solid solution.; Oxygen content above 0.8 wt % caused a sharp increase in hardness due to the formation of HfO2 particles.. Mechanism: The authors argue that oxygen contamination is the primary cause of embrittlement and prevents the formation of a single-phase random solid solution. The high oxygen content in MA powders leads to the formation of stable HfO2 oxides which cause brittleness. The single-phase bcc structure in the AT-SPS sample is attributed to the high cooling rate (~300 °C/min) during SPS, which suppresses the formation of secondary phases (bcc2 and hcp). Grain refinement and increased hardness in HPT-processed samples are caused by the formation of a high density of dislocations (>5 × 10^14 m^-2) and the presence of oxide particles in oxygen-rich samples.. Limitations: Swaging caused specimen cracking due to brittleness likely induced by high oxygen content (~0.75 wt %) or inappropriate deformation temperature/strain rate. The MA-SPS-HPT specimen broke into pieces during HPT, making its results disputable. Samples prepared by CIP and HIP retained considerable porosity and chemical inhomogeneities. The low hardness of HEAP-HIP samples could not be fully explained, though porosity and phase composition were suspected factors.. Future work: The authors state that the possibility of hot deformation of the alloy with increased oxygen content cannot be excluded under suitable conditions (i.e., low strain rate, or higher processing temperature), but this possibility needs more detailed study.. Quote: "The most promising result was obtained by SPS treatment of gas atomized powder with low oxygen content."

card: Paper card. Question: Can a low-temperature, rapid single-source precursor approach be used to synthesize a phase-pure, high-entropy 2D hexernary transition metal dichalcogenide (MoWReMnCr)S2 that exhibits enhanced hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) activity compared to 2H-MoS2?. System: Hexernary high-entropy metal disulfide (MoWReMnCr)S2; 2H-MoS2 (control); 20% w/w carbon black (CB) composite. Processing: Tandem thermal decomposition of five equimolar metal dithiocarbamate precursors (MoL4, WS(S2)L2, Re2(µ–S)2(L)4, MnL3, CrL3) at 500 °C for 1 h under argon flow (300 cm3 min−1); followed by liquid-phase exfoliation (LPE) in N-methyl pyrrolidine for 24 h with ultrasonication (37 kHz, 30% power) and centrifugation (1500 rpm, 3 h). Test conditions: HER electrocatalysis in 0.5 M H2SO4 electrolyte; Linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) at 5 mV s−1; Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) at −0.47 V vs Ag/AgCl; Chronopotentiometry at 10 mA cm−2 for 20 h; 7000-cycle CV stability test. Findings: The synthesized (MoWReMnCr)S2 contains 5.0 mol% Mn and 4.7 mol% Cr successfully incorporated into the 2H-MoS2 lattice, confirmed by pXRD and Raman spectroscopy.; Exfoliated nanosheets consist of 3–7 atomic layers with a homogeneous elemental distribution at the nanoscale, verified by HAADF-STEM and EDX mapping.; The (MoWReMnCr)S2@20%CB electrode achieved an overpotential of 229 ± 5 mV to reach 10 mA cm−2, significantly lower than the 362 mV for MoS2@20%CB.; The onset potential for (MoWReMnCr)S2@20%CB was −127 mV, compared to −219 mV for MoS2@20%CB.; The Tafel slope for (MoWReMnCr)S2 was 133.8 mV dec−1, indicating a Volmer-limited mechanism, compared to 152.9 mV dec−1 for MoS2.; Charge transfer resistance (Rct) for (MoWReMnCr)S2@20%CB was 3.12 Ω cm2, approximately eight times lower than the 25.11 Ω cm2 for MoS2@20%CB.; DFT calculations predicted that Cr and Mn substitutions activate the basal plane, reducing H adsorption energy (Eads) to near the optimal value of −0.24 eV.; The catalyst demonstrated high stability, retaining activity after 7000 CV cycles and 20 h of continuous operation at 10 mA cm−2.. Mechanism: The enhanced catalytic activity is attributed to the 'cocktail effect' where the high configurational entropy stabilizes the 2H phase and allows for the incorporation of Cr and Mn. DFT calculations suggest that substituting Mo with Cr and Mn activates the basal plane sites toward H adsorption, shifting the reaction mechanism to a Volmer-limited process with near-thermoneutral H adsorption energetics, while largely preserving the favorable electronic structure of MoS2.. Limitations: The study notes that the exfoliation process produced a size dispersion of nanosheets, and while purification to isolate monolayers is possible via liquid cascade centrifugation, it was beyond the scope of the current work. Additionally, the calculated electrochemically-active surface area (ECSA) using double-layer capacitance was deemed unreliable due to high frequency dispersion effects, requiring an alternative strategy using cyclic voltammetry.. Future work: The authors propose that the scalable synthesis approach is a universal route to produce 2D high-entropy materials of various transition-metal disulfides and that entropic stabilization of nanosheets is a powerful approach to produce 2D materials that cannot otherwise be produced due to intrinsic instability in the low-dimensional limit.. Quote: "A low‐temperature (500 °C) and rapid (1 h) single source precursor approach is successfully adopted to synthesize the hexernary high‐entropy metal disulfide (MoWReMnCr)S2."

card: Paper card. Question: Can high-throughput electrochemical screening results obtained from thin-film material libraries be reliably transferred to particulate catalysts for high-entropy oxide systems?. System: (Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni)3O4 high-entropy spinel oxides; compositional range (Cr8.1–28.0Mn11.6–28.4Fe10.6–39.0Co11.4–36.7Ni13.5–31.4)37.7±0.6O62.3±0.6. Processing: Combinatorial reactive sputter deposition on 100 mm Si/SiO2 wafers using a four-cathode system (Co, Cr, Fe, Mn50Ni50 targets) with Ar/O2 flow (80/40 sccm) at 0.4 Pa; deposition temperatures of 573, 773, and 973 K; target permutations used to disentangle correlated gradients. Aerosol-based synthesis for particles using metal nitrate precursors in ethanol, sprayed onto a deflector plate, dried in a 1073 K furnace, and annealed at 773 K in oxygen flow.. Test conditions: Thin films: Scanning droplet cell (SDC) in 0.05 M KOH, 3-electrode system, LSV 1–1.8 V vs RHE, 10 mV s–1 scan rate. Particles: Rotating disk electrode (RDE) in 1 M KOH, 1600 rpm, LSV measurements with iR-correction.. Findings: The most active thin-film composition identified was (Cr24.6±1.4Mn15.7±2.0Fe16.9±1.8Co26.1±1.9Ni16.6±1.7)37.8±0.8O62.2±1.2.; This hit composition exhibited an overpotential of 0.36 V at a current density of 1 mA cm–2.; The lattice constants of the single-phase spinel films ranged from 0.826 to 0.851 nm depending on composition.; The synthesized particles showed a composition of (Cr23Mn19Fe18Co25Ni15)-Ox with a diameter ranging from 75 nm to 1 μm.; The difference in overpotential between the thin film and the particle catalyst at 1 mA cm–2 was only 8 mV (thin film: 1.594 V, particles: 1.586 V vs RHE).; No correlation was found between surface roughness (Ra values of 1.2–4.8 nm) and electrochemical activity.; The highest OER activity was observed for compositions with high Cr, Ni, and Mn content, medium Co content, and low Fe content.. Mechanism: The authors argue that the observed activity trends are driven by compositional changes rather than microstructure or sheet resistance, as resistance maps and activity maps did not show the same trends. They state that since OER is a surface reaction, the kinetics at low overpotentials are governed by species adsorption, allowing for reliable comparison between thin films and particles despite different measurement geometries.. Limitations: The authors note that gradients of elements deposited from opposing targets are reversed, and neighboring targets have correlated gradients, which complicates the analysis of individual element contributions without the permutation method. They also mention that the low electrical conductivity of most oxide films required the use of a Pt electrode layer for SDC measurements, and that the resistance of the thin film variant B was not measured directly due to the underlying electrode layer.. Future work: The authors propose that combining theory, simulation, and machine learning with high-throughput experimentation can enable the prediction and understanding of new high-entropy materials, as no theoretical model currently exists that can reliably predict the electrochemical activity of HEMs.. Quote: "We demonstrate the successful transfer of results from thin-film material libraries to particles of Cantor alloy oxide (Co-Cr-Fe-Mn-Ni)3O4."

card: Paper card. Question: How can high-entropy materials (HEMs) leverage configurational entropy to overcome the limitations of conventional enthalpy-dominated catalysts, specifically regarding phase stability, active site tunability, and the breaking of scaling relationships in electrocatalysis?. System: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) including PtPdCoNiFeCuAuSn, PtPdRhRuCe, Ru0.44Rh0.30Co0.12Ni0.14, CoxMoyFe10Ni10Cu10, IrPdPtRhRu, Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni, and AlNiCoIrM; High-entropy oxides (HEOs) and perovskites; Multimetallic nanoclusters (MMNCs).. Processing: Carbothermal shock (ultrafast joule heating followed by rapid quenching at ~1500 K); Fast moving bed pyrolysis (FMBP) reaching 923 K within 5 s; Colloidal synthesis with seed-mediated coreduction and annealing at 600°C; Ionic liquid-assisted cosputtering; Ball milling and solvothermal synthesis.. Test conditions: Ammonia oxidation at 700°C; Ammonia decomposition at 500°C; Oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) in acidic and alkaline media; Oxygen evolution reaction (OER) in acidic and alkaline media; Hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) in acidic and alkaline solutions; Li-O2 battery cycling.. Findings: Quinary HEA nanoparticles (PtPdRhRuCe) achieved ~100% conversion and >99% selectivity toward NO + NO2 at 700°C with no degradation over 30 hours.; HEA-Co25Mo45 catalyst reached a mass-specific rate of 0.74 gNH3 m−2 hour−1 at 500°C, representing improvement factors of ~24 versus bimetallic Co-Mo and ~19 versus Ru.; Computational models predicted an IrPdPtRhRu HEA composition with a ~40-mV lower overpotential relative to Pt (111) for ORR.; Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni nanoparticles with size less than 2 nm delivered ORR activity comparable to Pt under the same conditions.; Octonary RuIrCeNiWCuCrCo catalyst outperformed quaternary and binary counterparts in long-term operation for Li-O2 batteries due to higher configurational entropy.; GO-supported quinary HEA nanoparticles (FeCoPdIrPt) exhibited enhanced HER activity and stability in alkaline solutions relative to commercial Pt/C catalysts.; HEA catalysts containing five or more elements outperformed binary, ternary, and quaternary alloys in alkaline media due to broad adsorption energy distributions.. Mechanism: Enhanced configurational entropy stabilizes single-phase solid solutions despite large enthalpic differences, allowing atomic mixing of multiple principal elements. Severe lattice distortion lowers the energy barrier for adsorption and activation, while the diverse local coordination environments and electronic perturbations (ligand effects) create a near-continuum distribution of adsorption energies. This distribution allows the catalyst to access optimal binding strengths for intermediates, breaking the linear scaling relationships that limit conventional catalysts.. Limitations: Low surface area of bulk HEAs limits catalytic utilization; maintaining nanoscale morphology at elevated temperatures is difficult due to migration and aggregation; synthesis of single-phase HEAs requires overcoming thermodynamic barriers; characterization is challenging due to increased compositional and structural complexities; phase segregation can occur if entropy is insufficient to overcome enthalpic differences.. Future work: Further elucidation of structure-property relationships across different HEM subcategories; development of high-throughput synthesis and measurement tools for accelerated materials discovery; deeper mechanistic studies on surface restructuring under reaction conditions; optimization of catalyst stability for noble metal-free applications.. Quote: "The ability to confine multiple principal elements in a single lattice is intriguing for the design of advanced catalysts with desirable activity, selectivity, and stability."

Paper card. Question: How can the configurational entropy in high-entropy alloys (HEAs) be leveraged to overcome the miscibility limitations of traditional alloys and enhance catalytic performance for complex reactions like ethanol oxidation?. System: Platinum-group metal (PGM) high-entropy alloy (HEA) nanoparticles containing Ru, Rh, Pd, Os, Ir, and Pt; specifically compared against physical mixtures of unary PGMs and binary/ternary/quaternary/quinary PGM alloys.. Processing: Prepared using a facile polyol method to synthesize PGM-HEA nanoparticles.. Test conditions: Electrochemical ethanol oxidation reaction in aqueous solution; performance compared against commercial Pd/C, Pd black, Pt/C, and Au@PtIr/C catalysts; cyclic voltammetry used to analyze individual constituent contributions.. Findings: The PGM-HEA nanoparticles exhibited much higher activity relative to commercial Pd/C, Pd black, and Pt/C catalysts.; Negligible activity was observed for the physical mixture of the six unary PGM nanoparticles, confirming the necessity of atomic mixing.; The PGM-HEA delivered a mass activity more than 1.5 times higher than that of the most active catalyst to date (Au@PtIr/C).; The PGM-HEA exhibited the highest current density in the full potential range compared to ternary, quaternary, and quinary PGM alloys.; Pt and Pd are active for ethanol conversion but become poisoned by adsorbed (CO)ad or CHx species.; Os and Ru facilitate the oxidation of (CO)ad, mitigating the poisoning effect for Pt and Pd.; Ir and Ru ensure that dehydrogenation or C─C cleavage occurs at a low potential, while further oxidation hinges on Pt and Pd components.. Mechanism: The atomically mixed metals in HEAs play distinct yet concerted functions: Pt and Pd drive ethanol conversion; Os and Ru mitigate poisoning by oxidizing adsorbed species; Ir and Ru lower the potential for C─C cleavage and dehydrogenation. This synergy allows for efficient and complete oxidation of ethanol involving multiple proton-electron transfers.. Limitations: The text notes that while simple reactions can be triggered by mono- and bimetallic PGMs, it is difficult to drive complex reactions involving multiple proton-electron transfers and intermediate species without the synergistic effects provided by HEAs.. Future work: The authors imply the need to better understand the contribution of each metal to the overall reaction, as demonstrated by their comparison of cyclic voltammetry curves of individual constituents to elucidate specific roles in preventing poisoning and facilitating cleavage.. Quote: "The PGM-HEA nanoparticles efficiently catalyzed the ethanol oxidation reaction, exhibiting a much higher activity relative to that of the commercial Pd/C, Pd black, and Pt/C catalysts, respectively."

card: Paper card. Question: How can the structural tunability of high-entropy materials (HEMs), specifically the antisite disordering and lattice distortion, be leveraged to optimize catalytic performance and energy storage capabilities compared to traditional alloys or compounds?. System: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) such as PtPdRhRuCe, CoMoFeNiCu, AlNiCoFeX; High-entropy oxides (HEOs) such as (MgCoNiCuZn)Ox, (CoCuMgNiZn)Ox, Li-containing entropy-stabilized oxyfluorides; High-entropy metallic glasses (HEMGs); High-entropy borides (HEBs), carbides (HECs), sulfides (HESs), and nitrides (HENs). Processing: Synthesis methods include carbothermal shock (CTS) with thermal shock at ~2,000 K within 55 ms; fast-moving bed pyrolysis (FMBP) heating to ~923 K within 5 s; ultrasonication-assisted wet-chemistry with local temperatures up to ~5,000°C; electrodeposition confining precursors to water nanodroplets within 100 ms; solid-state sintering; solvothermal synthesis; and mechanochemical methods. Test conditions: Catalysis tested at temperatures up to 1500 K and reaction temperatures of 305 °C or 155 °C for CO oxidation; electrocatalysis performed at ~80 °C in acidic and basic electrolytes; battery cycling at rates up to 2000 mA/g; supercapacitor testing in 1 m KOH solution at 100 mV/s scan rate. Findings: PtPdRhRuCe NPs achieved ~100% conversion and >99% nitrogen oxide selectivity for ammonia oxidation with no activity degradation.; Quinary CoMoFeNiCu NPs on carbon nanofiber showed a more than 20 times improvement in NH3 conversion rate versus Ru catalysts.; Co0.2Ni0.2Cu0.2Mg0.2Zn0.2O HEO achieved 98% conversion of benzyl alcohol in only 2 h under solvent-free aerobic oxidation.; Ni20Fe20Mo10Co35Cr15 HEA catalyst exhibited an overpotential of 107 mV in acidic solutions, comparable to Pt sheet.; Nanoporous AlCuNiPtMn exhibited a half-wave potential of 0.945 V in acidic media, representing a ~16-fold mass activity of Pt/C for ORR.; AuAgPtPdCu HEA catalyst achieved a faradaic efficiency of about 100% toward gaseous products at -0.3 V for CO2 reduction.; Rock-salt (Co0.2Cu0.2Mg0.2Ni0.2Zn0.2)O anode delivered an initial capacity of 446 mAh/g and 256 mAh/g after 100 cycles in a full cell.; Nanoporous AlCoCrFeNi HEA exhibited a high volumetric capacitance of 700 F/cm3 and excellent cycling stability of over 3,000 cycles.. Mechanism: The authors attribute enhanced performance to the 'high-entropy effect', 'lattice distortion effect', 'sluggish diffusion effect', and 'cocktail effect', which stabilize single-phase solid solutions and create diverse local electronic structures and adsorption energies. The large number of atomic sites allows tuning of surface electronic structures and adsorption energies, while the uniform configuration leads to severe lattice distortion that increases the activation barrier of diffusion, improving kinetic stability.. Limitations: The fundamental correlations between compositions and phases (e.g., phase diagrams) are not clear; the surface structures of HEMs may not be preserved at working conditions; productivity of HEA NPs via CTS is very low; the actual contribution of entropy versus enthalpy to Gibbs free energy is difficult to determine; and the surface structure of HEMs is more complicated than current catalysts.. Future work: Future work includes enhancing productivity for industrial applications, developing theoretical investigations using DFT and machine learning to design proper HEMs, achieving precise structural control of size, shape, and composition, developing 3D characterization techniques like electron tomography and APT, and exploring new types of HEMs with more than five elements.. Quote: "Precursor of metal salt mixtures was thermally shocked at ~ 2,000 K within 55 ms (as shown in Figure 2A), alloying up to eight dissimilar elements into single-phase solid-solution NPs"

card: Paper card. Question: How does the Direct Energy Deposition (DED) process affect the phase formation, microstructure, hardness, and thermal properties of Ti-Nb-Cr-V-Ni-Al refractory high-entropy alloys compared to thermodynamic predictions?. System: Ti-Nb-Cr-V-Ni-Al refractory high-entropy alloy (powders mixed at equal ratios to the phase analysis design), deposited on Ti-6Al-4V and Inconel 718 substrates. Processing: Direct Energy Deposition (DED) using a high-power diode laser (1000 W max, 780 W used), 980 nm wavelength, 3 mm spot size, 40% hatch overlap, 2 layers to 1 mm thickness, room temperature, sealed environment with Ar shield gas and N carrier gas. Test conditions: Microhardness measured via Vickers (9 indentations per area); Heat-Affected Zone (HAZ) analyzed via preheating test (500 W laser, 15 L/min Ar, 3 s duration); Microstructure analyzed via SEM, EBSD, XRD, and EDS. Findings: The actual microstructure contained sigma (σ), BCC A2, and Ti2Ni phases, differing from the predicted BCC A2, BCC B2, and Laves phases.; EBSD analysis revealed phase fractions of 64.2% σ phase, 28.2% BCC A2 phase, and 7.6% Ti2Ni phase.; The grain size of the deposited alloy was 1–35 μm, which is finer than the 45–150 μm powder size used.; The microhardness of the deposited Ti-Nb-Cr-V-Ni-Al was measured to be approximately 900 HV.; The microhardness of the Ti-6Al-4V and Inconel 718 substrates increased by 17–19% compared to wrought material due to heat treatment effects.; The HAZ depth of Ti-6Al-4V was reduced by 16.07% and Inconel 718 by 14.42% after deposition of the RHEA.; The σ phase peak intensity in XRD analysis was higher than those of the BCC A2 and Ti2Ni phases.. Mechanism: The microstructure growth and fine grain size are attributed to the high energy density of the laser in DED, which rapidly increases temperature and then causes rapid cooling, acting as a heat treatment effect. The high thermal diffusivity of the Ti-Nb-Cr-V-Ni-Al alloy reduces the heat-affected zone. The high hardness is related to the high volume fraction of the brittle σ phase.. Limitations: The accuracy of the phase analysis is highly dependent on the thermodynamic database used, and a complete thermodynamic analysis of each binary and ternary phase diagram belonging to the multicomponent system was not performed. XRD analysis generated significant noise caused by unmelted powder inside the deposited material.. Future work: The authors propose to analyze the effect of each process variable on phase formation and find suitable manufacturing conditions for RHEAs by controlling the process variables.. Quote: "The microstructure of Ti-Nb-Cr-V-Ni-Al showed that the BCC A2 phase, which grew first at high temperatures, grew first, and then the σ phase grew rapidly before the Ti2Ni precipitated phase grew."

card: Paper card. Question: What is the minimum level of thermodynamic assessment (specifically regarding ternary systems) required to correctly predict the thermodynamic properties and phase equilibria of quaternary high entropy alloys using CALPHAD?. System: Co-Cr-Fe-Ni (FAB=1, FAT=1), Co-Cu-Fe-Ni (FAB=1, FAT=1), and Al-Co-Ni-Ti (FAB=1, FAT=3/4). Processing: CALPHAD calculations using the TCHEA3 database; reference states (FAT=1 or 3/4) were compared against artificially reduced states (FAT=0) where all ternary interaction parameters were set to zero or ternary intermetallics were suspended, while binary parameters remained fully assessed.. Test conditions: Calculations performed at 800 °C for Co-Cr-Fe-Ni; 12,341 equally spaced system points with 2.5 at.% compositional steps were analyzed across the quaternary composition space.. Findings: In Co-Cr-Fe-Ni, 98% of fcc and bcc phase points calculated with FAT=0 matched the FAT=1 reference predictions.; In Co-Cu-Fe-Ni, only 63% of fcc phase points matched between FAT=0 and FAT=1 due to incorrect miscibility gap boundaries, while bcc phase agreement was nearly 100%.; In Al-Co-Ni-Ti, FAT=0 calculations failed to predict ternary intermetallic phases (H_L21, Laves_C14), filling those regions with binary phases instead.; Disagreements between FAT=0 and FAT=1 calculations occur primarily at or near the boundaries between different phase-field regions.; Systems with low density of phase boundaries (few intermetallics, no miscibility gaps) show negligible sensitivity to the removal of ternary descriptions.; The presence of ternary intermetallic phases in the system causes significant shifts in the composition and boundaries of neighboring phase regions when ternary interactions are neglected.. Mechanism: The accuracy of extrapolation depends on the thermodynamic properties of the subsystems; near-ideal mixtures (like Co-Cr-Fe-Ni) have negligible ternary contributions to Gibbs free energy, whereas systems with miscibility gaps or ternary intermetallics rely heavily on ternary interaction parameters to correctly define phase boundaries and phase stability.. Limitations: The study is limited to quaternary systems and relies on a single commercial database (TCHEA3); the authors note that locations of phase boundaries and ternary phases are unknown in novel composition spaces, making it difficult to apply these criteria a priori.. Future work: The authors propose that the conclusions for quaternary alloys can be extended to higher order systems, but emphasize that calculations using lower credibility databases require additional experimental verification.. Quote: "The main differences in the calculations occur at or near the boundaries between different phase fields. Therefore, higher density of these boundaries should result in lower accuracy of the FAT = 0 calculations."

card: Paper card. Question: Can a HfNbTaTiZr high-entropy alloy coating produced by electrospark deposition provide high corrosion resistance in aggressive saline environments compared to a stainless steel substrate?. System: HfNbTaTiZr high-entropy alloy (equiatomic composition) deposited on 316 stainless steel substrate. Processing: Mechanical alloying of high-purity Hf, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr powders for 60 h in a planetary ball mill with n-heptane as process control agent; consolidation via spark plasma sintering at 1000 °C, 50 MPa, and 100 hPa vacuum; electrospark deposition using Spark Depo Model 3 equipment under argon atmosphere. Test conditions: Electrochemical testing in 3.5% NaCl saline solution at room temperature; Open Circuit Potential (Eoc) measured for 6 h; Potentiodynamic polarization from −0.2 to +0.2 V at 1 mV/s scanning rate; Vickers hardness measured with 0.98 N load. Findings: The sintered bulk material achieved a density of 8.96 g/cm³, representing approximately 90% of the theoretical density of 9.9 g/cm³.; The deposited coating had a thickness of approximately 20 μm with a compact structure and no cracks at the interface.; The bulk consolidated sample exhibited a Vickers hardness of 840 HV.; The coating showed a corrosion rate of 0.00024 mm/year in 3.5% NaCl solution.; The coating demonstrated a more electropositive corrosion potential and lower corrosion current density compared to 316 stainless steel (icorr of 12.53 µA/cm²).; XRD analysis confirmed the main phase as body-centered cubic (BCC) with some very small FCC peaks in the coating.; Fine fissures were observed on the coating surface due to rapid cooling, but they did not penetrate the interface or significantly affect corrosion resistance.. Mechanism: The high configurational entropy and specific thermodynamic parameters (Ω ≥ 1.1, δ ≤ 6.6, VEC = 4.4) favor the formation of a stable BCC solid solution. The electrospark deposition process, performed under an argon atmosphere, produces high-purity coatings with low oxygen concentration. The rapid cooling during deposition causes fine surface fissures, but the compact nature of the layer and the formation of a passivation film (confirmed by oxygen presence in EDS) ensure good adhesion and corrosion resistance despite the thin film and minor cracks.. Limitations: The coating thickness was limited to approximately 20 μm, which could influence corrosion resistance; fine fissures are present on the surface due to rapid cooling and high hardness; the study was limited to 3.5% NaCl solution and did not test other aggressive media.. Future work: Future work will focus on optimizing electrospark deposition parameters to reduce cracking, depositing thicker layers, and testing in other chlorine-containing fluids such as geothermal fluids and in situ geothermal environments.. Quote: "The corrosion rate obtained after a test in chlorine containing fluid was very small (0.00024 mm/year)"

card: Paper card. Question: How do the phonon dynamics of the high-entropy alloy FeCoCrMnNi compare to those of glasses and complex metallic alloys (CMAs), and does it represent a unique class of materials?. System: Fe20Co20Cr20Mn20Ni20 (FeCoCrMnNi), a 5-element equiatomic FCC random solid solution. Processing: Polycrystalline samples produced by alloying high-purity elements in an inductively coupled high-frequency levitation furnace, slip-cast into a water-cooled copper mold, and annealed at 1200 °C for 48 h; single crystals grown via the Bridgman technique at 1340 °C with a solidification velocity of 50 mm/h under 200 mbar argon. Test conditions: Measurements performed at temperatures of 3, 15, 100, 200, and 300 K using inelastic neutron scattering (INS) and inelastic X-ray scattering (IXS); energy ranges up to 30 meV and wavevectors covering the Brillouin zone. Findings: Acoustic phonons propagate as well-defined modes throughout the entire Brillouin zone up to energies of 20–30 meV.; Phonon linewidths (ΓFWHM) are significantly broader than in simple monatomic elements but similar to binary alloys of the same constituents.; The observed phonon broadening is primarily attributed to force-constant fluctuations estimated at ~20%, while mass fluctuations contribute negligibly (<0.2 meV).; Phonon attenuation exhibits anisotropy, with longitudinal modes showing multiple regimes and transverse modes showing a smoother monotonic increase.; A strong scattering regime following ΓFWHM ∝ (ℏω)4.5±1 is observed up to ~18 meV in the [ζ00] direction, transitioning to (ℏω)1.7±0.2 above this energy.; The Ioffe-Regel limit (where mean free path equals wavelength) occurs only at energies above ~30 meV, much higher than in typical glasses.; The Generalized Vibrational Density of States (GVDOS) shows a linear dependence up to ~12 meV at low temperatures due to magnetic scattering, reverting to Debye-like (ℏω)2 behavior at room temperature.. Mechanism: The authors argue that the strong phonon attenuation is driven by force-constant fluctuations resulting from the random atomic environment, which are enhanced by the specific chemical disorder of the alloy. This mechanism is distinct from glasses where topological disorder is also present, and from CMAs where the acoustic phase space is reduced by optic modes. The authors note that the force-constant fluctuations per atomic pair (20–50%) are comparable to those in binary alloys, suggesting that increasing the number of elements from 2 to 5 does not necessarily increase phonon attenuation as predicted by some theories.. Limitations: The study notes that the strong incoherent neutron scattering entangled with the acoustic phonon in neutron data made the fitting procedure challenging for extracting linewidths, necessitating reliance on IXS data. Additionally, the theoretical models used could not reliably reproduce the low-q part of the spectrum due to the small supercell size used in simulations.. Future work: The authors propose that larger force-constant fluctuations should be sought by choosing elements with more different characteristics to effectively impact phonon engineering, noting that current HCP and BCC HEAs introduce stronger mass and atomic size disorder that prevents force-constant disorder from dominating.. Quote: "HEAs present unique phonon dynamics at the frontier between fully disordered and ordered materials, characterized by long-propagating acoustic phonons in the whole Brillouin zone."

card: Paper card. Question: What are the individual lifetimes and mean free paths of acoustic phonons in the clathrate compound Ba7.81Ge40.67Au5.33, and how do these properties explain its 'glass-like' low thermal conductivity?. System: Ba7.81Ge40.67Au5.33 (clathrate type I, space group Pm3¯n). Processing: Single crystal grown by the Bridgman technique; characterized by single-crystal X-ray diffraction and aberration-corrected TEM/STEM; bulk mosaicity less than 1 arcmin.. Test conditions: Neutron inelastic scattering (INS) on Time-of-Flight and Triple Axis Spectrometers at 300 K and 10 K; Neutron Resonant Spin-Echo (NRSE) technique used for high-resolution lifetime measurements up to 66 ps; thermal conductivity measured between 4 and 300 K using steady-state heat flow and 3ω techniques.. Findings: At 300 K, acoustic phonon mean free paths range from 120 nm at 2 meV (0.1 Å−1) to 21 nm at 4.4 meV (0.3 Å−1).; The phonon lifetime at E = 2 meV is 53(4) ps, corresponding to a mean free path of 120 nm.; At energies between 3.2 and 4.4 meV, phonon lifetimes are approximately 15 ps, with mean free paths of 31, 25, and 21 nm respectively.; The measured lifetimes are more than 10 times larger than the unit cell size (a = 1.08 nm).; A phenomenological model using only acoustic phonons and measured lifetimes yields a calculated lattice thermal conductivity of 1.2 W m−1 K−1, matching the experimental value of 1.1 W m−1 K−1.; Optical excitations (E2, E3, E4) have lifetimes of the order of 1 ps, with mean free paths as short as 1.5 nm.; The phonon lifetime at E = 3.8 meV decreases from 33(10) ps at 10 K to 15(1) ps at 300 K, while no temperature effect is observed at 2 meV.; State-of-the-art DFT simulations underestimate room temperature lifetimes and thermal conductivity by a factor of 3 to 5 compared to experimental data.. Mechanism: Thermal transport is dominated by acoustic phonons with long lifetimes traveling over distances of 10 to 100 nm; the lowest-lying optic mode acts as a 'low band pass' filter, suppressing acoustic states above ~4.5 meV and limiting the energy range for heat-carrying phonons. The authors argue that current simulations fail because they do not fully account for structural complexity, large chemical disorder, and potentially temperature-dependent force fields, leading to an overestimation of three-phonon scattering rates.. Limitations: The study notes that current computational limitations prevent simulations on supercells large enough to describe the observed disorder; the DFT simulations used an ideal ordered model which underestimates lifetimes; the low-temperature thermal conductivity behavior (T < 50 K) could not be fully explained without including boundary effects and other mechanisms like electron-phonon scattering.. Future work: The authors propose that future theoretical developments require advanced calculations, specifically atomistic or molecular dynamics simulations that take into account the detailed structural analysis including large disorder, and a possibly temperature-dependent force field to explain the non-trivial temperature dependence of 3-phonon scattering.. Quote: "Thermal transport is dominated by acoustic phonons with long lifetimes, travelling over distances of 10 to 100 nm as their wave-vector goes from 0.3 to 0.1 Å−1."
